metadata.title: Write Triggers, Not Topics.
metadata.subtitle: The Example Skill (Claude Plugins)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you write a description for a Claude Code skill, does naming its topic get it activated at the right moment — or does something else, its trigger phrasing, decide that? Lands the carry-out that a skill's description is the activation trigger Claude reads, not a summary of what the skill does.

beats.narration_text: People write it like a summary of what the skill does. That isn't the job. The description is the trigger Claude matches against a request. Does my skill's trigger description tell Claude when to use it?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 1.0 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('subject' -> 'trigger') lands on screen and the full corrected question finishes typing before the clip ends. NOTE: the trigger word was originally 'topic', which content_check.py's GATE CONTENT flags as a generic filler sentinel (_FILLER set) regardless of context -- changed to 'subject' to fix the actual content rather than loosen the validator. Parameters (42ms/char, 4% mistakeRate, 2% hesitateWithin, 8% hesitateBetween, 26% jitter) copied from the claude-plugins-official--claude-liam-agent-development sibling's own post-fix parameters (that reel's first attempt at 48ms/14%/6% ran out of its window on a similarly-sized text; this text is comparable length so the safe parameters are used from the start).

beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill actually is: one file — SKILL.md, in a folder under skills. The frontmatter has four fields. Name is the identifier, required. Description is the trigger, also required — and this is the one field they optimized for, because it's what Claude reads to decide whether to activate the skill at all. Version and license are optional metadata. A complex skill can add reference material, examples, and helper scripts in the same folder — but the minimum is just the one file.

Look at the template the docs give you: say it should be used when the user asks a specific phrase, mentions a keyword, or discusses a topic area. That phrasing is a tell. Claude is reading the description and deciding on its own whether the moment matches — nobody types anything to invoke it. Compare the other two shapes. A command only runs when a user types the slash — the trigger is the keystroke, not the language. An agent is something Claude spawns to handle a subtask — Claude picks it. Get the mode wrong, build a command when you needed a skill, and nobody ever sees it trigger.

production_viz.label: THREE ACTIVATION MODES
production_viz.caption: Claude activates it — nobody types or spawns it

beats.narration_text: Here's what's not in the docs: nothing explains how Claude actually matches your description against a request. No rule for length, no guidance on which phrases carry weight, no worked example of the match happening. The testing advice is just: check that your skill activates for expected queries. Which sounds fine until you look for how — there's no method, no sample query, no way to watch the match land. They kept SKILL.md's format brutally simple; the cost is the feedback loop. So most authors write a description, ship it, and never actually see whether it fires.

production_viz.label: WRITE IT, SHIP IT, HOPE
production_viz.caption: never actually see whether it fires

beats.narration_text: A skill's description isn't a summary of what it does — it's the trigger Claude reads to decide when to use it. Write it as an activation rule, not a topic blurb.

props.quote: A skill's description isn't a summary of what it does — it's the trigger Claude reads to decide when to use it. Write it as an activation rule, not a topic blurb.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm writing a Claude Code skill for a plugin that helps with database query optimization. Draft the SKILL.md description as an activation trigger, not a topic summary — the specific phrases a user might say, the keywords, the topic area — and add a short 'when to use' section with three example queries that should activate the skill and one that shouldn't. Then explain, field by field, why each phrase earns its place. Go deeper: ask the same model to write a second skill description that competes for the same activation moment, then judge which one Claude would actually match on — and what that says about where descriptions overlap in practice.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm writing a Claude Code skill for a plugin that helps with database query optimization. Draft the SKILL.md frontmatter description as an activation trigger, not a topic summary — include the specific phrases a user might say ('slow query', 'this join is scanning too much'), the keywords ('EXPLAIN plan', 'index', 'query planner'), and the topic area (SQL performance tuning). Then add a short 'when to use' section with three concrete example queries that should activate this skill and one that shouldn't. Finally, explain, one field at a time, why each phrase you picked earns its place as a trigger and not as documentation.
